extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal academics, patent lawyers, and policymakers interested in patent law and biotechnology
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze legal standards for patentability under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as applied to genetic materials and related methods, with emphasis on the Myriad decision and controlling precedent (Funk Bros., Chakrabarty, Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable under U.S. law an invention or discovery must satisfy three requirements: novelty, utility, and statutory subject matter (35 U.S.C. § 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This piece focuses on the third requirement (patent eligibility) rather than novelty or utility. Courts analyze §101 independently of novelty/utility inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: No one may patent 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a longstanding judicially created exception to §101 (cited from Chakrabarty and Diamond). If a claim is directed to such an exception it will be scrutinized for whether it adds something beyond the ineligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive name, character, or use requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patent eligible, an invention must have 'a distinctive name, character, or use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language (from Am. Fruit Growers, Inc. v. Brogdex Co.) is used to justify limiting patent protection so the law does not provide 'too much patent protection' and thereby impede progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature/purification doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Purification of a product of nature, without more, cannot transform it into patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Sweet and Supreme Court apply the rule that merely isolating or purifying a naturally occurring thing (e.g., DNA) is insufficient to render it patent eligible. Example: isolated DNA failed the test because its function and utility stemmed from naturally occurring nucleotide sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics test
rubrics_metrics.description: A product derived from nature is patent eligible only if it is 'markedly different' from anything found in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Diamond v. Chakrabarty: courts examine whether the claimed subject has markedly different characteristics or functions from natural counterparts. Applied to molecules (structure) or to uses/functions depending on the judge's approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure-based vs function-based 'markedly different' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Two analytical approaches exist: (1) focus on chemical/structural differences created by human intervention (Judge Lourie), or (2) focus on new and distinct uses/functions the claimed subject enables (Judge Moore).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different outcomes can follow depending on which approach is used: Lourie upheld claims based on chemical identity after isolation; Moore emphasized novel utility and uses rather than mere chemical change.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA treated as patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: cDNA (complementary DNA synthesized in a laboratory and lacking introns) is patent eligible because it is not naturally occurring and is 'distinct' from native DNA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court held that 'the lab technician unquestionably creates something new when cDNA is made.' This supports patentability of lab-synthesized molecules that do not exist in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated genomic DNA ineligibility (Myriad holding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated DNA molecules are not patent eligible because the chemical changes from isolation were not what the patent claims were 'articulated in terms of' or dependent upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court rejected deference to PTO practice and held that merely isolating native DNA did not produce patent-eligible subject matter when the claimed invention's utility derived from the natural sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: mental processes and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Method claims that are essentially mental processes of analyzing and comparing are not patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Sweet invalidated certain method claims because they involved mental processes; courts will scrutinize whether a claimed method is merely an abstract/mental process or adds inventive subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo framework for process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes that amount to 'little more than a description of natural laws' are not patent eligible (Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Mayo, a claim that merely applies a law of nature using routine, conventional steps fails §101 because it effectively monopolizes the natural law. Courts look for an 'inventive concept' beyond the natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity undermines eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that rely on 'well-understood, routine, conventional activity' already engaged in by researchers are less likely to be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Bryson (and Mayo) emphasized that adding routine steps to a natural law does not transform it into patent-eligible subject matter; courts will consider whether the asserted invention involves more than ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing for declaratory judgment in patent suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff has standing only if there is 'meaningful preparation to conduct potentially infringing activity' — i.e., a real and imminent injury from the patent right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit found only plaintiffs who alleged immediate plans to engage in potentially infringing BRCA-related activities had standing; suits by those without a sufficiently real threat may be dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO practice and judicial non-deference absent Congressional endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: A PTO's longstanding policy of granting certain patents (e.g., isolated DNA) does not require courts to defer unless Congress has endorsed that view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court refused to grant deference to the PTO's practice in Myriad because Congress had not expressly authorized the PTO's interpretation and the Justice Department opposed it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding policy-based expansion of §101 by courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should focus on statutory rules and precedent rather than try to resolve deep policy disputes about incentives for innovation; legislative action is the better forum for crafting industry-specific solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses institutional constraints on the judiciary: reconciling competing incentives (private investment vs free flow of information) is primarily a legislative task (e.g., prizes, compulsory licensing, tax incentives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption and chilling effects as evaluative considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad patent exclusivity that can enjoin a wide range of research or impose crippling litigation costs will be scrutinized for its chilling effect on research and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs argued that upholding broad gene patents would prevent further discovery, increase costs dramatically (example comparing testing costs), and chill nonprofit research; courts consider these practical effects when reasoning about §101 limits, even if policy solutions belong to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent application (Funk Bros. and Chakrabarty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court and lower courts use Funk Bros. (product of nature/purification denied) and Chakrabarty (engineered organism patentable as 'markedly different') as principal precedents for analyzing patent eligibility of biological subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts must identify which precedent better fits the claim: whether the claimed subject is merely a natural phenomenon/purified natural product (Funk Bros.) or a human-made invention with markedly different characteristics (Chakrabarty).
